items.heading: Counselling, in the Sense Most
items.text: Counselling, in the sense most people search for it, centres on assessment and one decision: aptitude, interest, and work-style signals read together, then applied to a specific fork, which stream, which course, whether to take a specific offer or pivot. Used well, that is a real and useful input into a career plan, not a wasted step.

items.heading: The Gap Shows Up
items.text: The gap shows up in a specific way: a counselling session closes with a decision, and a decision on its own does not tell you what happens in year two or year three. Someone counselled into the "right" stream or the "right" first skill can still drift for years afterward with no milestones to check progress against and no sequence for what comes after that first choice.

items.heading: Whether It's Called Counselling
items.text: Whether it's called counselling or planning, these are the things worth checking before you book.

items.heading: A Real Career Plan Needs
items.text: A real career plan needs more than one resolved decision: milestones you can check yourself against, and a skill portfolio sequenced across time, not just a direction to feel good about today.

items.heading: If Your Actual Question
items.text: If your actual question is narrow and immediate, a counselling-style session is the right, sufficient tool, don't pay for planning-level structure you don't need yet.

items.heading: Paid Support, Whichever Label IT
items.text: Paid support, whichever label it carries, earns its cost once the decision or the plan gets expensive, time-pressured, or hard to reverse alone.
